summary: Medicare Shared Savings Program Accountable Care Organizations Performance Year 2025 Financial and Quality Results Medicare Shared Savings Program (Shared Savings Program) Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) are critical in helping Make America Healthy Again — by supporting high-quality, coordinated care that addresses prevention, chronic illness and the root causes of disease. The Shared Savings Program’s unique design means ACOs are held accountable for saving money and improving healthcare quality, delivering a win for both patients and the Medicare Trust Funds. The Shared Savings Program is one of the largest programs in the country that aims to reduce overall costs of care while ensuring Medicare beneficiaries receive high-quality care. For Performance Year (PY) 2025, ACOs in the Shared Savings Program achieved the highest rates of shared savings since the inception of the program. Out of 472 ACOs, 80% of ACOs, representing 84% of the 10.9 million assigned beneficiaries, are earning performance payments totaling $4.9 billion, and Medicare saved $2.5 billion relative to benchmarks. PY 2025 had the highest share of ACOs receiving performance payments and the highest amount of savings for ACOs and Medicare since the inception of the Shared Savings Program. Financial Results ACOs had higher gross per capita savings in PY 2025 compared to PY 2024, $690 vs $643, respectively. However, ACOs had lower net per capita savings in PY 2025 compared to PY 2024, $234 vs $241. The decrease in net per capita savings represents more ACOs moving into two-sided risk tracks (a 4 percentage point increase between PY 2024 and PY 2025), and ACOs participating in two-sided tracks are eligible for higher shared savings rates and, therefore, can retain more of the savings they earned. Gross per capita savings are the savings shared by ACOs and Medicare, whereas net per capita savings represent the savings for Medicare only. Low revenue ACOs continue to outperform high revenue ACOs, generating $300 vs $169 net per capita savings. Typically, low revenue ACOs are physician-led ACOs or are comprised of federally qualified health centers and/or rural health centers, while high revenue ACOs are hospital-led. Additionally, ACOs composed predominantly of primary care clinicians had higher performance compared to ACOs with fewer primary care clinicians, with $417 vs $208 in net per capita savings. In its first PY (PY 2025), the 24 ACOs participating in the CMS Innovation Center’s ACO Primary Care Flex (ACO PC Flex) model generated $652 in gross per capita savings and $186 in net per capita savings. Notably, 92% of PC Flex ACOs (22 of 24) earned shared savings, compared with ~80% of all Shared Savings Program ACOs. The difference between gross and net per capita savings reflects, in part, that 88% of PC Flex ACOs participate under the ENHANCED track, which offers the highest shared savings rate, and that 33% of PC Flex ACOs are new ACOs. The ACO PC Flex model has a Prospective Primary Care (PPC) Payment option to shift payment for primary care away from fee-for-service, visit-based payment to a flexible, predictable revenue stream. PC Flex ACOs also performed well on quality measures, comparable to similar Shared Savings Program ACOs. Twenty-nine eligible ACOs received advance investment payments (AIPs), intended to provide advanced shared savings for upfront investments to build the infrastructure needed to succeed in the Shared Savings Program and address beneficiary needs. Twenty-five AIP ACOs shared in savings totaling $46 million, and as part of this financial reconciliation cycle, we will recoup $22 million of these advance payments from AIP ACOs that earned shared savings. ACOs that achieved savings had lower utilization compared to their benchmark across many categories of utilization including hospital discharges, Emergency Department (ED) Visits, number of Skilled Nursing Facility (SNF) stays, and SNF Utilization Days. Thirteen ACOs owed shared losses totaling $23 million. Quality Results All ACOs reported the new Alternative Payment Model (APM) Performance Pathway (APP) Plus quality measure set in PY 2025 and met quality reporting requirements under the Shared Savings Program. Adoption of all-payer digital quality measures (electronic clinical quality measures [eCQMs]) and Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) clinical quality measures (CQMs) also increased from PY 2024. CMS continues to encourage ACOs to move toward reporting digital quality measures using electronically stored and transmitted health information, leveraging interoperability, reducing burden, and improving efficiency. Medicare Clinical Quality Measures for ACOs participating in the Medicare Shared Savings Program (Medicare CQMs) became the most commonly reported collection type in PY 2025. Additionally, 264 ACOs reported at least one Medicare CQM in PY 2025, compared to 64 ACOs in PY 2024. ACOs that reported Medicare CQMs in both PYs 2024 and 2025 showed significant improvement on measures of controlling blood pressure, glycemic status assessments, and rates of depression screening with a follow-up plan. Shared Savings Program ACOs helped more patients improve markers of good health, such as controlled blood pressure and diabetes management, compared to 2024. Among ACOs that reported quality measures as eCQMs, the mean percentage of beneficiaries with adequately controlled high blood pressure increased significantly from PY 2024 to PY 2025 (from 71.21% to 73.86%). Among ACOs that reported eCQMs, the mean percentage of beneficiaries with poorly controlled diabetes (glycemic status assessment greater than 9%) declined significantly from PY 2024 to PY 2025 (from 28.36% to 24.63%). Nearly all ACOs outperformed similar types of physician groups on quality measures: ACOs performed significantly better than comparable physician groups on eCQMs for Screening for Depression and Follow-up Plan (55.03% among ACOs versus 50.64% among comparable MIPS groups) and Controlling High Blood Pressure (73.86% among ACOs versus 70.38% among comparable MIPS groups). ACOs have performed consistently better than comparable physician groups on the patient experience survey measure, Getting Timely Care, Appointments, and Information for every year that the survey has been fielded since 2019. Calendar Year 2027 Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule Updates The Trump Administration is committed to ensuring that ACOs’ participation in the Shared Savings Program promotes better chronic disease management and prevention, more efficient use of resources and innovation, and drives increased savings for the Medicare Trust Funds. To advance these goals, in the Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) Final Rule released on Nov. 4, 2026, and effective Jan. 1, 2027, CMS finalized policies that will strengthen incentives for ACOs to join and remain in the program, expand accountable care relationships for beneficiaries, improve the accuracy of financial benchmarks and beneficiary assignment, reduce administrative burden, and advance digital quality measurement and interoperability. Among these policies, the creation of a new growth adjustment to the historical benchmark will create a financial incentive for ACOs to recruit providers who are new to Medicare shared savings initiatives and serve beneficiaries who have not previously participated in accountable care relationships. These policies also provide opportunities to increase shared savings payments; ACOs in level E of the BASIC track will see their shared savings rate increase from 50% to 60%, and ACOs that already generate strong savings through the prior savings adjustment will have opportunities to increase shared savings payments with the prior savings adjustment’s scaling factor increasing from 50% to 75%. Additionally, starting Jan. 1, 2027, ACO-participating clinicians will have the option to receive higher payment for office visits with additional complexity, recognizing the added investments ACOs make in care coordination and giving clinicians a direct, meaningful financial incentive to join or remain in an ACO. CMS is also updating our beneficiary assignment policies to expand the number of beneficiaries eligible for the Shared Savings Program, while reducing gaming opportunities. Additionally, CMS is finalizing changes to the quality reporting requirements to: extend availability of a MIPS CQM collection type and extend the associated MIPS CQM reporting incentive, extend the use of flat benchmarks to score Medicare CQMs, revise the Shared Savings Program quality reporting requirement to allow ACOs to exclude ACO Participant TIN(s) from the ACO’s quality data submission under certain circumstances, revise the definition of a beneficiary eligible for Medicare CQMs to align with an ACO’s assigned beneficiary population, establish the Medicare eCQMs collection type to further support ACOs in the transition to dQM reporting, revise the Shared Savings Program scoring policy for excluded measures or measures that lack a benchmark, halt plans for ACOs to report more quality measures, and simplify Shared Savings Program certified electronic health record technology (CEHRT) use requirements. Lastly, Shared Savings Program ACOs, for the first time, will have the option to reduce or eliminate beneficiary cost sharing for certain Part B services, giving ACOs a direct, tangible benefit to offer the patients they serve and strengthening the beneficiary engagement case for healthcare providers joining or starting an ACO.
